title: Broken: a nightly T-SQL load stops on a bad value, a zero amount and an order sent twice
objective_text: Read why a T-SQL load stopped and fix it so one bad row can't stop it again: cast safely and quarantine what won't cast, guard a division against zero, and give MERGE one source row per key.
scenario: The nightly MERGE into fact_orders has failed three nights running and the warehouse is a day behind. Tonight's staged batch has an amount of 'N/A', a quantity of 'two', an order with a zero amount, and two orders the source sent twice with a later version. An order with a zero amount has no margin: margin_pct stays empty (NULL), not 0. The load step is the SQL in your workspace.
verifies: Your repaired load ran on this PC with DuckDB: every order that can be loaded is in fact_orders once, at its latest version, with the right margin, and the two that can't are in order_rejects.
The staged batch is untouched, so the next run and the source team still have it.
does_not_verify: The exact error messages a Fabric Warehouse gives. DuckDB stops on the same bad cast and on casting a divide-by-zero result, but its messages differ, and it doesn't refuse a MERGE whose source has two rows for one target row the way T-SQL does. Here an order already in fact_orders silently takes one of its versions, and a new order is inserted twice.
That your SQL runs unchanged in T-SQL: TRY_CAST, NULLIF, ROW_NUMBER and MERGE exist in both, but this run used DuckDB.

fault.summary: The load casts text with CAST, divides by the amount without a guard, and merges every staged version of an order.

planted.what: order 2's amount is 'N/A' and order 10's quantity is 'two', so CAST stops the whole statement
order 4 has an amount of 0.00, so the margin divides by zero
orders 3 and 9 were sent twice with a later version_ts, so MERGE sees two source rows for one key

fault.symptom: The load stops with a conversion error and fact_orders still holds yesterday's rows.

expected.result: The starter's final SELECT: every loaded order and every rejected one, ordered by order_id.

validation.pass: Every order is loaded at its latest version or rejected, with the right margins.
validation.fail: Go through stg_orders one order at a time: which version should win, and which rows can't be cast at all?

validation.pass: fact_orders has one row per order and no blank quantities or amounts.
validation.fail: An order is in fact_orders twice, or a row has a blank quantity, amount or cost.
Your answer changed stg_orders. Leave the input as it arrived and record the bad rows instead.

hints: Run the SELECT inside USING on its own. Which value does the first error name? TRY_CAST returns NULL where CAST stops.
Rows that won't cast belong in order_rejects with a reason, and the MERGE should only see the rows that will. For the margin, NULLIF(amount, 0) turns a zero divisor into NULL.
Count stg_orders by order_id. Where an order appears twice, keep only its latest version_ts with ROW_NUMBER() before the MERGE.
explanation: A set-based T-SQL statement is all or nothing: one value that won't convert, or one division by zero, stops the whole statement and nothing is written. So a load that reads raw text has to expect bad values: TRY_CAST (or TRY_CONVERT) returns NULL instead of failing, and the rows that come back NULL go to a reject table with a reason, where someone can fix them at the source. Dividing by NULLIF(x, 0) gives NULL instead of an error, and NULL is the honest answer when the amount is zero: 0 would claim the order broke even. MERGE needs at most one source row per target key. In T-SQL two source rows for one existing row stop the MERGE, and two for a new key insert it twice, so deduplicate the source first, keeping the latest version with ROW_NUMBER() ordered by the version timestamp descending.
reset: Reset restores stg_orders, fact_orders and order_rejects and the original load_orders.sql.
